title: The Language and Writing System of MS408 (Voynich) Explained
venue: Romance Studies 37(1): 30-67; accepted author manuscript in the University of Bristol research repository
proposes_language: proto-Romance (an unattested ancestor of the Romance languages of Mediterranean Europe)
summary: Cheshire argues that the manuscript is written in an extinct 'proto-Romance' language with its own alphabet of unfamiliar and familiar symbols, no dedicated punctuation, all lower case, no double consonants, and many multi-vowel abbreviations for phonetic components, with some Latin words and abbreviations. He holds that the language's lexicon survives scattered across the modern languages of Mediterranean Europe, and presents the language and writing system so that others can read the manuscript. The repository page links the open accepted author manuscript; the publisher's version is behind Taylor & Francis.
established: The paper states nine features it attributes to the text (extinct language, mixed unfamiliar and familiar symbols, no dedicated punctuation, symbol variants marking punctuation and accents, lower case only, no double consonants, diphthong-to-quintiphthong abbreviations, some Latin words); these are the author's analysis, matched by comparison of proposed readings with words in modern Romance languages and Latin, not by a held-out or controlled test.

The author proposes a sign-to-sound alphabet and word readings built from it, and names the language only as proto-Romance, an ancestor whose lexicon he says is now dispersed among the modern Mediterranean Romance languages.

open.question: Since 'proto-Romance' has no surviving corpus, does Cheshire's alphabet, frozen as a substitution key, read the hidden pages better than its decoys against the closest attested period Romance corpora (Latin, Italian, Catalan, Occitan, Spanish, Portuguese)? Openly licensed text: no corpus exists for the proposed language itself; period proxies are openly available (e.g. Catalan: public-domain early editions of Ramon Llull, several hundred thousand characters; Old Occitan troubadour texts on Wikisource, cc-by-sa; Italian and Latin already on the grid).
open.check: Encode the paper's alphabet as a fixed key (no search budget) and score it against each proxy language with the usual decoys.

open.question: Add the missing period Romance proxies the proposal leans on (Catalan, Old Occitan, Galician-Portuguese) as corpora so the grid can test this family at measured power.
open.check: Kind corpus, >=150,000 characters each, open licence stated at the source.
